progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b10 (route level only: "Define cases, population and time window"; "Calculate and compare rates without mixing denominators"): incidence, prevalence and mortality, each a count out of a population over a time. From s05: equation, substitute, solve, sense check ("One E and three S's"). From b11 (settled order): observational and intervention designs, cross-sectional and cohort studies, bias, confounder, the four-step frame (design, strength, limitation, judgement). From b07: UV exposure and melanoma (Q2's context only). From Year 11 Working Scientifically: independent and dependent variables, graph conventions. s06 (graphs and data, with TAILS) sits in the Chemistry playlist only (route change 10), so TAILS is spoken once with its meaning here, as a recall for Chemistry viewers and new for Biology viewers. Not assumed: age-standardised (glossed in 2c as "adjusted as if both regions had the same age mix").
progression.startsWith: Epidemiology questions in the HSC tend to ask for three things. Calculate a rate from new data, draw a graph of rates, and judge whether a study supports its claim. Here are three HSC-style questions, one of each. Pause and try each one properly, then we'll work through it together.
progression.stopsAfter: calculating incidence (550 and 700 per 100,000 per year) and mortality (25 and 36 per 100,000 per year) for two regions and evaluating a raw-count claim, with age structure named as the check before inferring risk; constructing a line graph of melanoma incidence and mortality rates on one set of axes (year on the x axis to scale, rate per 100,000 per year on the y axis from 0 to 60, both series with a key and a title) and describing and explaining the two trends (incidence rising then levelling; mortality far lower and falling; early detection and removal, more skin checks, consistent with better treatment); calculating prevalence in a survey (9 and 4 per cent), naming the design (cross-sectional), and evaluating it (quick, measures prevalence; cannot show which came first, confounders, self-report, one city; association only; a cohort would be stronger).
progression.nextLesson: how type 2 diabetes can be managed (bio-m8-b12).

teaching.task: When an exam gives you disease counts, a table of rates or a study with a claim, how do you calculate the rate, draw the graph and judge the claim?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why raw counts mislead (a bigger population gives more cases at the same risk; 2c, 2d); why age matters (diabetes rises with age, so an older population has a higher crude rate; 2c); why one y axis works and why it starts at zero (same unit; every value must fit; 3b, 3d); why the years are spaced to scale (time is continuous; 3b); why points are joined (each is a whole year's rate; 3b); why melanoma mortality is far below incidence (early detection and removal; 3c); why same-year deaths and diagnoses don't give survival (different people; 3c); why a snapshot can't show cause (no order in time, confounders; 4c); why sample size reduces random uncertainty but doesn't remove selection bias or fix design (4d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Epidemiology questions in the HSC tend to ask for three things. Question one. Rates first, laid out as equation, substitute, solve, sense check. Now the claim. The classic mistake is comparing raw counts. Question two. Set up the graph before you plot anything. Now describe and explain. The classic mistake is starting the y axis at thirty, to fit the incidence line. Question three. Prevalence is existing cases out of the group, as a percentage. Now the limitations. The classic mistake is thinking two thousand people makes the claim proven. So, here's your first move for each type.
teaching.openingDecision: Epidemiology questions in the HSC tend to ask for three things. Calculate a rate from new data, draw a graph of rates, and judge whether a study supports its claim. Here are three HSC-style questions, one of each. Pause and try each one properly, then we'll work through it together.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a). Q2's card adds a line inviting a longer pause for drawing. Nothing answer-bearing during the holds.
teaching.curriculumScope: - B8-IQ2-02: "collect and represent data to show the incidence, prevalence and mortality rates of non-infectious diseases, for example:" with the listed examples "nutritional diseases" and "diseases caused by environmental exposure". Q1 calculates incidence and mortality rates (type 2 diabetes, a nutrition-linked disease); Q2 represents incidence and mortality rates as a graph (melanoma, a disease caused by environmental exposure); Q3 calculates prevalence from survey counts. "Collect": Q3's survey is the collected data, and Q2's table is secondary data.

design.visualSystem: One practice board throughout, in M7 g01's and g03's layout: top-left the question card (stem, data and demands as an exam prints them, with the "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience" tag), readable through the whole question; the working fills the right two thirds; a type badge top-right ("Calculate rates", "Draw the graph", "Judge the study"), hidden during each attempt. When the walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to a strip and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card). Earlier questions are cleared before the next card writes on. Q1's working is s05's step rows (equation, substitute, solve, sense check) with M7 g01's DenominatorPair showing the population boxed under each fraction, then two small coded rate bars (P and Q side by side per 100,000) beside a pair of population blocks drawn to scale (P eight times Q). Q2's working is the coded GraphPaper (lesson-local): a faint grid on which the axes, ticks, labels, points, lines, key and title draw stage by stage on their cues, with s06's TailsRail in the side column. Q3's working is a coded two-group dot field (400 and 1,600 dots, cases tinted) beside the prevalence rows, then b11's four-slot frame strip (design, strength, limitation, judgement). Plates: m8-pancreas-v1.png (Q1 card), m8-skin-melanoma-v1.png and m6-uv-skin-v1.png (Q2 card and 3c), m5x-clipboard-sheet-v1.png and new m8-energy-drink-can-plain-v1.png (Q3 card). No people, hands or faces: residents, survey respondents and patients are words or plain coded dots only. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
design.transitionPlan: heading "Calculate it, graph it, judge it" writes on. fresh board. the card shrinks to a strip; type badge "Calculate rates". the calculation rows dim; the answer table stays. a chip "6600 > 1050, so P is worse" writes on and, on "the classic mistake", takes a grey scribble cross. board clears. the card shrinks to a strip; type badge "Draw the graph". the TAILS rail dims. a small inset graph draws beside the finished one with its y axis from 30 to 60: the incidence line looks steep and the mortality points sit below the axis, cut off (label "mortality missing"). board clears. the card shrinks to a strip; type badge "Judge the study". the dot fields shrink and dim. a chip "2000 people, so it's proven" writes on and, on "the classic mistake", takes a grey scribble cross. the board becomes two columns, "What you see" and "What you do first", each row lighting on its cue with its question number badge: "counts from groups of different size → rate per 100 000, same unit for all (Q1)" with the population blocks thumbnail; "a table of rates to graph → axes, units, even scale that fits every value, then plot (Q2)" with the graph thumbnail; "a study and a claim → name the design; association or cause? (Q3)" with the frame strip thumbnail. > Here are the key notes.

scenes.visualReference: the card shrinks to a strip; type badge "Draw the graph". GraphPaper fills the working area (faint grid). s06's TailsRail builds in the side column, rows lighting on cue (grey tag "s06: TAILS"). On "x axis" the horizontal axis draws, label "Year" (violet; "Year" underlines amber in the table header); rail row A lights. On "y axis" the vertical axis draws with the label "Rate (per 100 000 people per year)" (amber; "per 100 000 people per year" underlines in both headers); rail row L lights. On "five" the x ticks write at their true positions: 1985, 1995, 2005, 2015, then 2020 half a step on (a small bracket "5 years" under the last gap); rail row I lights. On "zero to sixty" the y ticks write 0, 10, 20 ... 60 and "52" in the table underlines (label "even steps; fits 52"); rail row S lights. On "Plot each point" the incidence points drop one by one (teal crosses, each table cell underlining as its point lands), then the mortality points (amber crosses near the bottom); on "ruled line" each set joins with straight segments, incidence teal, mortality amber (grey tag "each value is a whole year's rate: join point to point"). On "key" a small key writes ("incidence", "mortality"); on "title" the title writes above the grid: "Melanoma incidence and mortality rates in Australia, 1985 to 2020", with the grey caption chip "illustrative data, based on the pattern of Australian statistics" under it (it stays on the completed graph); rail row T lights. On "TAILS" the rail's five letters pulse once. At most three bright text items besides the graph. Hold 1 second.
